title: Design a Price Feed
statement_md:
*Gang of Four pattern: **Observer** (behavioural). The feed announces that a
price moved. What anything listening does about it — or how many things are
listening — is none of the feed's business.*

Implement `PriceFeed`, a price ticker that subscribers attach themselves to.

- `PriceFeed()` — start with nothing attached.
- `subscribe(name, symbol, kind, arg)` — attach a subscriber called `name`,
  watching `symbol`, reacting according to `kind`. Returns `True`, or `False`
  if it was rejected (below).
- `unsubscribe(name)` — detach `name`. Returns `True` if it was attached,
  `False` otherwise.
- `publish(symbol, price)` — announce a price, and return the names that raised
  an alert, **in notification order**.
- `count()` — how many subscribers are attached.
- `subscribers()` — the attached names, in notification order.
- `alerts(name)` — the alerts `name` has raised, as `[symbol, price]` pairs in
  the order they happened, or `null` if `name` was never registered.

**Notification.** Subscribers are notified in the order they were attached. A
subscriber is notified of an update only if `symbol` matches what it watches —
either the same ticker, or `"*"`, which watches everything. A subscriber that is
not notified is not affected by the update at all: it does not count towards its
own tally, and it does not remember the price.

**The four kinds.** Each subscriber remembers, per symbol, the last price it was
notified of — updated on every notification, whether or not it alerts.

| `kind` | `arg` | raises an alert when… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"threshold"` | a price level | `price` is at or above the level **and** the last price it was told for this symbol was below it, or it has been told none. A move that stays above the level does not alert again; dropping below and coming back does. |
| `"drop"` | an amount | it has been told a previous price for this symbol, and `price` is at most that previous price minus the amount. |
| `"every"` | a count $k$ | this is the $k$-th, $2k$-th, … notification it has received, counting all symbols together. |
| `"limit"` | a count $c$ | always — and immediately after its $c$-th alert it **detaches itself**. |

A subscriber detaching itself in the middle of a `publish` must not disturb the
rest of that pass: everything attached after it is still notified. Afterwards it
is gone — later publishes skip it, `count()` no longer includes it,
`unsubscribe` on it returns `False` — but its alert history survives, and
`alerts(name)` still returns it.

**Names are spent once used.** `subscribe` returns `False` and changes nothing
if `name` has ever been registered, even if it has since detached. It also
returns `False` if `kind` is not one of the four above, if `symbol` is neither
`"*"` nor one to five uppercase letters, or if `arg` is below the smallest value
its kind allows — `0` for `"threshold"`, which is a price level, and `1` for the
other three, which are counts and amounts.

**Complexity.** `publish` is $O(s)$ where $s$ is the number of attached
subscribers, plus a further $O(s)$ for each `"limit"` subscriber that
reaches its cap during the call and detaches itself. `subscribe` and `count`
are $O(1)$, `unsubscribe` is $O(s)$, `subscribers()` is $O(s)$, and
`alerts(name)` is $O(a)$ in the number of alerts it returns.

With `desk` watching `"*"` on `"every"` 1, `alarm` watching `AAPL` on
`"threshold"` 100 and `dip` watching `AAPL` on `"drop"` 5, publishing
`AAPL` at 98, 101, 104 and 96 returns `["desk"]`, `["desk", "alarm"]`,
`["desk"]` — 104 is still above 100, so there is no new crossing — and
`["desk", "dip"]`.
constraints: $0 \le \texttt{symbol.length} \le 7$; a valid one is `"*"` or one to five uppercase letters.
`publish` is always called with one to five uppercase letters as its symbol.
At most $200$ distinct names are used.
At most $10^4$ calls will be made to `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `publish`, `count`, `subscribers`, and `alerts`.

solutions.title: One Feed That Knows Every Kind of Subscriber
solutions.intuition_md:
Keep the subscribers as rows in the feed's own tables — `kind`, `arg`, `scope`, the per-symbol memory, the tally, the alert log, one dictionary each keyed by name — and put the reaction rules in `publish`.

The loop then reads exactly as the specification does: for each attached name in order, skip it if the symbol does not match, update its memory, and then ask, in a chain of branches, whether *this* kind alerts on *this* update. Four kinds, four branches, one place to look.

That last part is also the problem. The feed is now the only thing that knows what a subscriber is for, so every subscriber's behaviour is written into the object that is supposed to be merely announcing prices.
solutions.algorithm_md:
`subscribe` validates and then writes one row into each of six tables. `unsubscribe` and the self-detach path both go through `_detach`, which drops the name from `active` and from the ordered list.

`publish` walks a **copy** of the order list. This is not optional: a `"limit"` subscriber detaches itself in the middle of the pass, and removing an element from a list you are iterating makes the loop skip the element after it — the classic way this problem is got wrong. The `name not in active` guard covers the same hazard from the other direction.

The branch chain is the part worth looking at. `"threshold"` needs the previous price to tell a crossing from a level; `"drop"` needs it to measure against; `"every"` needs a tally; `"limit"` needs neither but has a lifecycle. Four rules with four different state requirements, and all four sets of state live in the feed's tables whether or not a given subscriber uses them — a `"limit"` subscriber still carries a `last` dictionary it never reads.

What this costs is felt on the next change. A fifth kind means a new branch in `publish`, a new minimum in `subscribe`'s validation, and — if it needs state none of the others do — a seventh parallel table that every other kind now also carries. Nothing about the code points at all three places.
solutions.time_complexity: O(s)\text{ per publish plus } O(s)\text{ per self-detach, } O(1)\text{ per subscribe}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: `publish` looks at every attached subscriber once and does constant work per subscriber — a dictionary read, a comparison, maybe an append. `subscribe` is a handful of dictionary writes. `unsubscribe` and a self-detach are $O(s)$ because removing a name from the ordered list scans it — so a publish in which $k$ `"limit"` subscribers all reach their caps costs $O(s \cdot k)$, not $O(s)$. Keeping a position index instead would make each removal constant, at the price of either tombstones or an index rebuild, which at $200$ names is not worth the complication; the statement charges for it rather than pretending it away.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Six table entries per name ever registered, plus the per-symbol memory each one accumulates, plus the alert logs — $A$ alerts in total across all subscribers, which are kept after a detach because `alerts(name)` still has to answer.

solutions.title: Observer (The Feed Announces, The Subscribers Decide)
solutions.intuition_md:
Invert who knows what. Give each kind of subscriber its own class with one method — `update(symbol, price)`, returning whether it alerted — and let the feed do nothing but call it.

Now the reaction rules sit next to the state they need. `ThresholdObserver` holds a level and the previous price; `EveryObserver` holds a tally; `LimitObserver` holds a cap and knows when it is finished. Nothing carries state for a rule it does not have, and `publish` has no idea any of it exists — it iterates, calls `update`, and collects the names that said yes.

This is the pattern's actual claim, and it is about direction rather than effort: the subject depends on an interface, the subscribers depend on nothing, and adding a subscriber does not modify the subject.
solutions.algorithm_md:
`Observer` fixes the shared part of every rule — remember the last price per symbol, count the notification, append to the log when the rule fires — and leaves one abstract question, `fires(symbol, price, prev)`. Each subclass answers it in a line.

`LimitObserver` is the interesting one, because its rule is not about the price at all but about its own lifetime. It overrides `update` rather than `fires`, calls up, and sets `done` when it has had enough. The feed checks `done` after every notification and detaches. That one flag is the entire protocol for a subscriber that wants out — the feed does not know why, and does not have a `"limit"` branch anywhere.

`KINDS` maps a kind string to a class, so `subscribe` constructs rather than branches. The validation minimum — `0` for a price level, `1` for a count — is the one place a kind is still special-cased, and honestly it belongs on the class; it is here to keep the two solutions line-comparable.

What has *not* changed is the copy in `publish`. Iterating a snapshot is required by self-removal, not by the branching, and the first solution needs it just as much. It is worth being clear about that, because "use Observer" is sometimes offered as the fix for the skip-a-neighbour bug, and it is not.

The payoff is the fifth kind: a new class, a new line in `KINDS`, nothing else touched, and no other subscriber given state it does not use. The cost is five classes where six dictionaries and a branch chain would do — for four fixed kinds the first solution is genuinely easier to read start to finish, and the indirection only earns its keep when the set of subscribers is open rather than closed.
solutions.time_complexity: O(s)\text{ per publish plus } O(s)\text{ per self-detach, } O(1)\text{ per subscribe}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Identical to the first solution. A virtual call to `update` costs what the branch chain cost, and the same subscribers are visited in the same order. What moved is where the rule is written, not how much work runs — this problem's two approaches differ in structure, and the clock cannot tell them apart.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: One object per name ever registered instead of six table rows, holding only the fields its own rule needs — a `"limit"` subscriber carries a cap and a counter rather than a per-symbol memory it never reads. The alert logs dominate either way and are kept after a detach.
